analysis.one_liner: Caps federal income tax for lower- and middle-income earners and adds a surcharge on income above $1 million.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2026 with 21 Democratic and independent senators behind it, but has taken no action since it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the basic income tax for working households. It would set a cap — an alternative maximum tax — so that a single filer earning under about $80,500 pays no more than 25.5% of the portion of income above a cost-of-living exemption (about $46,000 for a single person), which effectively zeroes out federal income tax below that level; couples and heads of household get higher thresholds. To pay for it, the bill would add a surcharge on individuals with income above $1 million: 5% on the next million, 10% up to $5 million, and 12% beyond that, on top of their existing taxes. Both changes would take effect for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Single filers with income under roughly $80,500, joint filers under roughly $161,000, and heads of household under roughly $112,700. Anyone below the cost-of-living exemption (about $46,000 single, $92,000 joint, $64,400 head of household) would owe no federal income tax at all under the cap; earners above it would have their tax capped at 25.5% of income above the exemption, cutting typical bills by hundreds to thousands of dollars.

how_it_helps.text: For a qualified single filer (income under 175% of the cost-of-living exemption, about $80,500), federal income tax could not exceed 25.5% of income above the exemption — roughly $46,000, adjusted for inflation [S2].
Income below the exemption (about $46,000 single, $92,000 joint, $64,400 head of household) carries a maximum tax of zero, eliminating federal income tax for filers at those levels [S2].

The cost is shifted to high earners: an additional surcharge of 5% on income over $1 million, 10% over $2 million, and 12% over $5 million, with joint filers getting 50% higher thresholds and all thresholds inflation-indexed [S2].
The surcharge is on top of existing tax and cannot be used to reduce other taxes or offset the alternative minimum tax, and the inflation-indexed thresholds keep it from eroding over time [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with modified adjusted gross income above $1 million (about $1.5 million for joint filers), who would pay the new 5-12% surcharge in addition to their regular income tax. Corporate income is not touched, and the surcharge base is reduced by any investment interest deduction, a small carve-out for leveraged investors.

drawbacks.text: The benefit cuts off sharply: a single filer just under the roughly $80,500 eligibility line gets the tax cap, while a filer one dollar over it gets nothing, creating a large cliff at the boundary [S2].
The surcharge base is defined as income reduced by the investment interest deduction, so high earners who borrow to invest get a lower surcharge than those with wage income at the same level [S2].

The cost-of-living exemption and surcharge thresholds are indexed from the CPI-U level at enactment, so the real value of both the tax cut and the surcharge's revenue depends on how inflation behaves from the start date [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a full income tax exemption plus a capped rate for working households, funded by a surcharge on income above $1 million. The main design flaw is the hard cliff at the eligibility cutoff, which gives a large break to someone earning $80,499 and nothing to someone earning $80,501 — a smoother phase-out would avoid that. The investment-interest carve-out in the surcharge base is a modest leak favoring leveraged investors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 12, 2026 and referred the same day to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Chris Van Hollen introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, joined by 19 other Democratic and independent senators including Sanders, King, Booker, and Gillibrand [S2].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced; that referral is the last action in its history [S4].

The bill has two operative parts: an alternative maximum tax capping income tax for lower- and middle-income filers, and a new surcharge on individuals earning over $1 million, both effective for tax years after December 31, 2025 [S2].
No Republican senators cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-led Senate Finance Committee has not scheduled a markup or vote [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed, which favors the status quo: households earning over $1 million continue to pay no surcharge while the bill sits without a committee vote. Workers would benefit only if the bill advances.

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Working Americans' Tax Cut Act on March 12, 2026.

for.name: 20 Democratic and independent senators (incl. Sanders and King)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction; all 20 are Democrats or independents.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Committee received the bill on referral and has not scheduled a markup or committee vote since.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits with the Republican-chaired Finance Committee.

industries.note: The bill would put a 5-12% surcharge on income above $1 million, with joint filers getting higher thresholds. Their gain under the status quo is the tax revenue the bill would redirect to working households.

industries.industry: Leveraged investors who deduct investment interest
industries.note: They would owe the surcharge like other high earners, but the bill defines the surcharge base as income reduced by the investment interest deduction, shrinking their bill relative to wage earners at the same income.

analysis.trajectory: Standalone tax bills without any Republican cosponsorship rarely get a markup in the Senate Finance Committee. Unless Democratic leadership folds the proposal into a broader tax package, it will most likely sit unacted upon and expire when the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
